A.explanation: This is the ratio $(640-600)/1240 = 0.032$ without multiplying by $g$. Weight difference, not mass difference, provides the resultant force.

B.explanation: The net weight $(640-600)g$ accelerates the total mass $1240 \text{ kg}$, giving $a \approx 0.32 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.

C.explanation: This results from dividing the $40g$ resultant force by only the $640 \text{ kg}$ counterbalance instead of the total $1240 \text{ kg}$ being accelerated.

D.explanation: This results from dividing the $40g$ resultant force by only the $600 \text{ kg}$ loaded car instead of the total $1240 \text{ kg}$ being accelerated.

hints: Notice the loaded car mass is $520 + 80 = 600 \text{ kg}$ while the counterbalance is $640 \text{ kg}$, so the counterbalance side is heavier by $40 \text{ kg}$.
Think of the two weights acting in opposite directions over the pulley, so the resultant driving force is the difference of the weights $(640-600)g$.
Apply $F = ma$ to the whole system: the driving force must accelerate both masses together, so divide by $600 + 640 = 1240 \text{ kg}$.
walkthrough: Add the passenger to the car: $m_{car} = 520 + 80 = 600 \text{ kg}$. The counterbalance mass is $m_{c} = 640 \text{ kg}$.
Because the pulley is light and frictionless, the tension $T$ is the same on both sides and both masses share the same magnitude of acceleration $a$.
The resultant force on the system is the difference in weights: $F = m_{c}g - m_{car}g = (640 - 600)g = 40g$.
With $g = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$, $F = 40 \times 9.81 = 392.4 \text{ N}$ acting to pull the counterbalance down and the car up.
Use Newton's second law for the total mass moved: $F = (m_{c} + m_{car})a$, so $a = F/(m_{c} + m_{car})$.
Substitute values with units: $a = 392.4 / (640 + 600) = 392.4 / 1240 \approx 0.32 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
